A2.text:
Aysel is twenty-three. Last week, she started a new job. She is a parking inspector in the centre of Baku. Her job is to enforce the parking law. Cars without a permit must get a fine.

On her first day, Aysel saw a white car near a school. It did not have a permit, and parking there was forbidden.

Then she saw the driver. It was Mrs Sabina, her old English teacher!

“Aysel! How nice to see you,” Mrs Sabina said. “I only stopped for five minutes. Can you bend the rules for me?”

Aysel did not know what to do. Nobody was watching. She could get away with it. But it was not fair to the other drivers.

At that moment, an angry man came. “This car is in front of my shop again!” he shouted. “I will let the air out of the tyres!”

“No,” Aysel said. “You cannot take the law into your own hands. That is my job.”

The shopkeeper was a witness. Aysel wrote the fine. Mrs Sabina was quiet. She paid and drove away.

A week later, Aysel got a card. It was from Mrs Sabina. It said: “I am proud of you. You learned more in my class than English.”

Aysel smiled and put the card in her bag.

B1.text:
Aysel had been a parking inspector in central Baku for exactly one week. The job was simple on paper: check permits, enforce the law, write a fine for any car parked where it was forbidden. In practice, she was learning, every driver had a story.

On Friday morning she found a white Hyundai parked across a pavement outside School Number 23. No permit. A sign right above it said “No parking, 8:00–18:00.”

She was taking a photo of the number plate when a woman rushed out of the school gates. Aysel recognised her immediately: Mrs Sabina, her English teacher from years ago, who had once kept her after class for talking too much.

“Aysel? My goodness, look at you in uniform!” Mrs Sabina smiled warmly. “Listen, I was only inside for five minutes. Technically, the rule is for parking, and I was just stopping. Surely that's a loophole? Couldn't you bend the rules, just this once?”

For a long moment, Aysel didn't answer. The street was nearly empty. Nobody would ever know; she could easily get away with it. But that morning she had fined a taxi driver and a young mother for exactly the same thing. It wouldn't be fair.

Before she could decide, the owner of the shop next door marched out. “Every single day this car blocks my door!” he shouted. “Next time I'll let the air out of the tyres myself!”

“Please don't,” Aysel said firmly. “You can't take the law into your own hands. That's what I'm here for.”

The shopkeeper agreed to act as a witness. Aysel wrote the fine and handed it over. Mrs Sabina read it, nodded without a word and drove away.

A week later, an envelope arrived at the parking office with Aysel's name on it. Inside was a card in familiar handwriting: “You did the right thing, and you did it kindly. I'm proud of you. P.S. You still talk too much.”

B2.text:
Aysel had been a parking inspector in central Baku for precisely seven days, long enough to discover that the job, though straightforward on paper — check permits, enforce the law, issue a fine wherever parking was forbidden — was in reality a daily masterclass in human excuses. Everyone, it turned out, had been “just two minutes”, and everyone's two minutes were uniquely justified.

On Friday morning she came across a white Hyundai straddling the pavement outside School Number 23, directly beneath a sign that read “No parking, 8:00–18:00”. No permit on the dashboard.

She was photographing the number plate when a woman hurried out of the school gates, and Aysel's stomach dropped. Mrs Sabina — her English teacher from years ago, the woman who had once kept her behind after class for talking through an entire lesson on the present perfect.

“Aysel! Look at you in uniform!” Mrs Sabina's delight seemed entirely genuine. “Now, I was only inside for five minutes. Strictly speaking, the sign prohibits parking, and I was merely stopping — that's a loophole, surely? Couldn't you bend the rules, just this once, for an old teacher?”

Aysel hesitated. The street was all but deserted; nobody would ever find out, and she could get away with it effortlessly. Yet only that morning she had fined a taxi driver and a young mother with a pushchair for exactly the same offence. Letting this one go wouldn't be generous — it would simply be unfair.

The decision was taken partly out of her hands when the owner of the neighbouring shop stormed onto the pavement. “This car blocks my door every single morning!” he bellowed. “Next time, I'm letting the tyres down myself!”

“I'd strongly advise against that,” Aysel said, more steadily than she felt. “You can't take the law into your own hands. That's precisely why I'm here.”

The shopkeeper, mollified, agreed to serve as a witness. Aysel completed the fine and handed it over. Mrs Sabina scanned it, inclined her head without a word of protest and drove away.

A week later an envelope addressed to Aysel arrived at the parking office. Inside was a card in instantly recognisable handwriting: “You did the right thing, and you did it with grace. Rules mean nothing if they only apply to strangers. I'm very proud of you. P.S. You still talk too much.”
